theory: Orion never toured here because the Aussie radio relays aren't easy to control. That's my theory and I'm sticking to it.

theory.t: After the fire on 9 September 1989, Marcus Hale vanishes. Funny how an architect disappears right when the building burns. I reckon he planned the exit.

theory: Fourteen lines, ten-ish pressings. Do the maths. Each region got its own bit. I'm not guessing line 14, but I reckon whoever finds it will get a surprise.
Our little corner of the world sits under the Southern Cross, far from Orion's usual targets. Maybe that's why the Aussie pressing is cleaner.

theory.t: The 'well-earned rest' in December 1989 sounded dodgy to me. Nobody who never leaves the studio needs a holiday.

theory: If you slow the tape down a touch, the carrier shifts down too. So it's baked in. That's about as close to proof as I've got.

theory.t: I bought 'Glass Hours' on a whim. Played it three times looking for the carrier. Nothing. Not a whisper. Luna's a different thing.

theory: Radio folk in the bush talk about odd signals. Probably nothing. But the same old blokes say Nova's carrier sounds a bit like a numbers station.
Whatever Nova is, someone put a lot of work into hiding that 14.2 Hz tone. You don't do that for a joke.

theory.t: The Akasaka tapes in May 1995 changed everything. That whisper at the end of the reel, so soft you'd miss it, and so strange I can't stop playing it.

theory: Think about it: a singer who only exists on a satellite feed. Not on stage, not on a street. Makes you wonder who's on the other end.

theory.t: Memo 89-117 popped up online in 1993 and named a director. Whoever Kalen is, I want his side of the story.

theory: Might be wrong, but I reckon the hidden message is about passing something on, not about hiding something.
Cassette hiss is just noise. The carrier is not noise. Learn the difference and you'll start hearing it too.
A bloke at uni who does DSP said it looks like a BPSK carrier. I nodded like I understood. I've been reading ever since.

theory.t: The Hamburg broadcast in June 1985 froze for three minutes while the sequencer kept playing. Either a glitch or a message. I vote message.

theory: Most theories are rubbish, mine included. But rubbish theories lead to better ones, so keep 'em coming.
If Orion's lawyers are still sending out letters, someone's still worried. That tells me plenty.

theory.t: The cease-and-desist to Ashford Poly in 1994 only made mirrors spring up everywhere. Orion's lawyers sure helped spread it.

theory: My mate swears the carrier is a lullaby. I reckon it's a countdown. We agree it's weird.
Think about the name 'Stardust'. Dust gets everywhere, and so does the signal.
One day someone will find line 14 and we'll all say 'oh, of course'. Until then, I'm listening.
I used to think this was all a prank. Then I saw the graph. Now I'm not so sure.
It doesn't matter whether it's real. The community is real. That's the bit that counts.
Honestly I've no idea. But I'm having a ripper time finding out.

where_i_was.t: 18 March 1985, SYNTHESIS drops. I was {age_then}, saving pocket money, and didn't get my hands on a copy until months later at a record fair.
8 June 1985, Hamburg. The time difference meant I heard about it at school on Monday. Three minutes of silence, and everyone had a theory by lunch.
13 July 1985, Live Aid. We watched it all night on telly, sleeping bags on the lounge floor. Nova wasn't on, and I remember thinking that was weird.
9 September 1989. A 'small electrical fire' made two paragraphs in some overseas paper. A mate in the States posted me the clipping. It's on my wall.
9 November 1989, the Berlin Wall. The whole world was glued to the news. I was too, but half my brain was on a certain singer who'd gone quiet.
9 December 1989, the last broadcast. Late on every cue, looking off camera. I taped it off a satellite feed at a mate's place. We didn't say much after.
15 December 1989: 'resting'. I read that and knew it was rubbish. The next morning I started a list of everyone who agreed.
March 1990, I posted a postcard to the Orion Tower: WHERE IS NOVA? Cost me a stamp and a bit of pride. No reply.
12 April 1990, 'Glass Hours'. A friend bought it and played it at a barbie. Everyone liked it. I went and sat in the car.
I found out about the fan network in 1993 through a uni lab in {city}. It was the first time I'd ever typed a message to a stranger overseas.
9 September 1993, Listening Night I. No modem yet, so I sat in the dark with a radio and a clock, waiting for 02:14 UTC. Dog barked, nothing else happened. Best night of my life.
9 September 1994, Listening Night II. I had a dial-up login by then and watched 614 people appear in an IRC channel. I typed 'g'day' and got ignored. Fair enough.
22 May 1995, the Akasaka tapes hit the net. I started the download on Friday and it finished on Sunday. Phone bill was horrific.
9 September 1995, Listening Night III. {n} of us online. I'd moved my 486 to the lounge room so I could hear the stereo, and Dad kept walking through. I swear I heard something at 02:14.
1 March 1996, the 'Free the Masters' petition. I signed from the uni lab at 11pm. One of 18,402. Felt tiny and proud at once.

spectrum: Pulled a Triple J off-air tape into the PC and ran an FFT. The 14.2 Hz peak sits roughly {db} dB above the floor. No dramas spotting it once you know where to look.
I checked the tape on two decks. The line didn't move, so it's not my gear. Good news for science.
Sampled at 44.1 kHz, {secs} seconds. The peak is thin and steady, like a pin stuck in the graph.
A bloke from my uni DSP class took a squiz. Said it looks like deliberate modulation. That's as far as he'd go.
Mains hum here is 50 Hz, nowhere near 14.2. So the spike isn't power noise.
Compared the Festival pressing to a dub. Same spot, same strength. Repeatable.
I ran the program three times on three different tapes. Same result. Either it's real or my software has a sense of humour.
I don't have a scope, only software. Take the numbers with a grain of salt, like you would a pie from a servo.
The line gets stronger in the quiet sections. Makes sense: nothing to hide behind.
Tried to decode it as BPSK. Got gibberish. Probably my fault, not the signal's.
I'll upload the graphs when I find a scanner. Promise.
